subject: principles-of-accounts
title: Absorption and Marginal Costing: Where the Fixed Overhead Goes
objectives: Build both unit costs layer by layer: $20 under marginal costing and $32 under absorption costing
Explain why closing inventory carries fixed overhead forward under absorption costing only
Reconcile absorption profit of $9,400 with marginal profit of $7,000 by the $2,400 deferral

definitions.meaning: A costing method that attaches all production costs, variable and fixed, to units: here the unit cost is $32, including $12 of fixed production overhead per unit.
A costing method that attaches only variable production costs to units: here the unit cost is $20, and fixed production overhead is charged to the period.
Production cost that does not vary with output: here $12,000 for 1,000 units produced, which is $12 per unit.
The production cost attached to one unit: $20 under marginal costing and $32 under absorption costing for the same product.
The units produced but unsold at the period end: here 200 units, which under absorption costing carry $2,400 of fixed overhead forward.
Sales revenue minus variable costs: here 800 x ($50 - $20) = $24,000, the starting point of the marginal costing profit.
A cost charged in full to the period in which it is incurred: fixed production overhead is a period cost under marginal costing, but not under absorption costing.

mechanismSteps: Both unit costs build from the same three variable layers: direct materials $10, direct labour $6 and variable production overhead $4 land in both columns, giving a variable cost of $20 per unit (s1).
Fixed overhead lands only in the absorption column: $12,000 over 1,000 units is $12 per unit, taking the absorption unit cost to $32 while marginal costing routes the $12,000 to the period (s2).
Closing inventory carries $2,400 of fixed overhead forward: 200 unsold units x $12 under absorption costing, while marginal costing expenses the full $12,000 in this period (s3).
Absorption profit is higher by exactly that $2,400: marginal profit is $7,000 and absorption profit is $9,400, separated only by the deferral in closing inventory (s4).
workedExample: Reconcile the two profits for one product. Step 1 (s1): build the variable layers - direct materials $10 + direct labour $6 + variable overhead $4 - so the marginal unit cost is $20. Step 2 (s2): fixed production overhead is $12,000 over 1,000 units, so $12 per unit lands only in the absorption column and the absorption unit cost is $32. Step 3 (s3): production of 1,000 less sales of 800 leaves closing inventory of 200 units, and those units carry 200 x $12 = $2,400 of fixed overhead forward under absorption costing. Step 4 (s4): marginal profit is $7,000 (contribution $24,000 - $12,000 - $5,000) and absorption profit is $9,400, so absorption profit is higher by exactly that $2,400 deferral.

trap.misconception: Absorption and marginal costing always report the same profit, because fixed production overhead is a period cost under both methods.
trap.explanation: The slip: Fixed production overhead is a real production cost either way, so it is easy to assume both methods must charge it to the same period and the choice of method cannot change profit. The fix: The methods differ on timing: marginal costing expenses the full $12,000 of fixed production overhead in the period, but absorption costing attaches $12 per unit to inventory, so the 200 unsold units carry 200 x $12 = $2,400 of fixed overhead forward in closing inventory - which is why absorption profit of $9,400 exceeds marginal profit of $7,000 by exactly that $2,400 deferral. In class, replay scene 3: freeze on the closing inventory of 200 units and ask where their $12 per unit of fixed overhead has gone under each method - expensed under marginal costing, carried forward under absorption costing.
